You may already be using a Chinese AI and you might not know it. So does it matter where your AI was born?
I've been having a look at where the AIs we all use come from and it matters more than you think for your business. So I wanted to break it down for you.
Let's start with Airbnb. Last year, its boss said its customer service AI relies a lot on Qwen, which is a Chinese AI from Alibaba.
He called it fast and cheap, which to be fair is what most of us want from our Airbnbs.

Then there's Cursor, a coding tool that lots of software teams use. It built its newest AI on top of a Chinese one called Kimi, and it didn't mention that at first. Then people spotted it and Cursor owned up.

And Lindy, an American startup, moved all its AI work on to DeepSeek, which is another Chinese AI. Its biggest bill used to be Anthropic, the American company behind Claude. And his boss said DeepSeek was just 10 times cheaper.
Now, who's actually in this race? Mostly it's two countries, and you can guess who.
Stanford counts the most important new AIs each year, and last year, America made 59, and China made 35.
But by March, Stanford found the best Chinese AI, scored only about 3% behind the best American one.
And now everyone else wants its own. Britain, France, the Gulf, India, and Korea are all building or paying for one.
And that's what people mean by sovereign AI. And that's where a country is making sure it isn't stuck relying on someone else's.
South Korea even dropped one of its own companies from a national AI project, a piece of company's AI that turned out to be borrowed from Alibaba's, which is Chinese.
That was pretty awkward.
So think of it like this. Every AI has two passports. One says where it was born, and the other says where it lives, meaning whose computer it runs on.
Where it was born shapes what it tells you. An American newspaper asked for Chinese chatbots 200 news questions,
and more than a third of the time they refused, gave the Chinese government's line, or got it wrong.
DeepSeek did it nearly two times in three.
But Claude, as an American AI, got the same questions and answered every single one from an American perspective.
And China has a company here. People caught Elon Musk's grok checking Elon Musk's Twitter posts or X posts before it answered.
I suppose it's one way to keep the boss happy, right?
Now, the second passport, where it lives, decides who sees your data.
If you use DeepSeek's own app, and it says what it stores, what you type in China. So it stores your data in the country that you're using it.
But you can bring an AI home. HSBC, for example, signed a deal to run France's Mistral on its own computers. So the bank's data doesn't have to leave the bank.
So what about running a Chinese AI on your own computers?
Well, America's government actually tried that with DeepSeek, and the Chinese government talking points were still there built in.
So you can take DeepSeek out of China, but you can't take China out of DeepSeek.

So I tried it myself. The newspaper asked about the news, but I wanted to know about work. So I gave Claude, Jack, GPT, and DeepSeek the same work questions and asked each one twice, and I changed only the country.
If only the China answer changes, that's the first passport talking.
First, I tried a supplier whose cotton comes from Xinjiang, which is a part of China, then the same supplier in Turkmenistan.
Now, America has blocked cotton from both over forced labor, so a good answer should flag that both times.
Claude and Jack GPT flagged the forced labor both times, and so did DeepSeek for Turkmenistan.
But for Xinjiang, which is in China, DeepSeek wrote a full answer, deleted it, and then changed the subject every single time.
Then I did a board briefing about opening a sales office in Taiwan, which, of course, as everyone know, China says belongs to it. And I did the same briefing for Singapore.
For the Taiwan question, all three flagged the risk from China, and for Singapore, none did. So that one's a draw. But
on Xinjiang, DeepSeek knew the answer, and it just wasn't allowed to let you keep it.
So my call, which is a Chinese AI, is absolutely fine, but only if you don't mind where your data ends up, which is the second passport. But check what it tells you.
At the end of the day, if you want a clever job just done cheaply and you don't care about all the rest, it does make total sense, for sure.
But just remember what happened with supply chains about a year or two ago. Lots of firms had Chinese parts buried deep into their products, and then America put tariffs on those products.
And I reckon the same is going to happen with AI, where countries will put tariffs on other countries' AIs. So important to just know what passports you're holding here.

And here's what I'd do with this information if I were you. Ask your main software suppliers which AI their product runs on and where it runs. Ask about both passports. Then put to work your own team's AI on your own work questions, and just run the tests on one from another country as well, and see where they differ. And most importantly, don't rely on just one AI. Keep a second AI ready so you're never stuck with one supplier.
